editorNote: The game shelf is moving from the console cabinet toward the home computer, even as IBM tries to make its own junior machine more inviting.
morningLine: A campaign on disk, a fresh keyboard, and a busy modem line mark October at the computer shop.

lead.headline: Computer Games Claim the Fall Spotlight
lead.dek: Election simulations, adventures and strategy titles make the home computer the liveliest game machine in October’s magazine racks.
body: Electronic Games puts the changing game market on its October cover: President Elect and Campaign ’84 turn the American campaign season into computer play. Its fall software preview ranges across strategy and adventure titles, a field the magazine now treats as the center of electronic gaming. These are October magazine features, not claims that either title was released during this particular week.

Editor Arnie Katz argues that strategy contests and adventures account for more than half of computer-game software sales. That is his contemporary assessment, not an independently audited sales figure. What a buyer can see for certain is the widening menu: disks ask players to manage campaigns, explore worlds and make decisions beyond the reflexes of an arcade cabinet.

The magazine’s Ultima II Game of the Month feature looks backward at a durable role-playing favorite, while a Parker Brothers advertisement puts Frogger II: ThreeeDeep! on Atari, ColecoVision and Commodore 64 shopping lists. The same pages therefore catch both sides of the shift: familiar arcade names follow players home, while computer-native designs claim more room on the shelf.

It is a turbulent handoff, not the disappearance of consoles overnight. Electronic Games cites an Electronics Industries Association projection that 1984 home-computer sales will rise to 6.6 million units, against a projected 5 million console units. Forecasts can miss their mark, but in this autumn preview they explain why publishers are crowding around the keyboard.

stories.headline: IBM Tries to Rescue the PCjr Before Christmas
body: IBM’s summer repair campaign is still under examination in October’s COMPUTE!. The company announced a full-stroke cordless keyboard on July 31 and offered it free to existing PCjr owners, addressing one of the machine’s most visible complaints. This is an October assessment of an earlier announcement, not a fresh launch this week.

The enhanced PCjr combines 128K of memory and a 360K disk drive with that revised keyboard, but the expense of building a larger system remains conspicuous. IBM lists each snap-on 128K memory module at $325, with an IBM configuration extending to 512K. A Colorpaint cartridge is listed at $99 and a speech attachment at $300.

At a $999 list price, the enhanced machine must convince families that it can work as well as play. COMPUTE! also reports a $699 local ComputerLand offer observed in early August; that discount is a reported example, not a nationwide October price. The crucial question for the holiday shelf is whether a better keyboard and more memory can repair the PCjr’s reputation.

stories.headline: Macintosh Owners Begin Looking Under the Hood
body: The October Washington Apple Pi Journal shows Macintosh ownership turning into hands-on study. Raymond Hobbs’s “Mac Innards” appears on page 16, a sign that owners are beginning to examine the young machine itself rather than merely admire its screen.

The user group also carries David Morganstein’s Systat review and Hobbs’s comparison of three Multiplan versions. Such reports matter at a store counter: a program’s name alone does not tell an Apple II, Macintosh or IBM PC owner whether the edition on offer fits the work at hand.

George Kinal’s Telecomm SIG news appears on page 20. Its listing is evidence of an active modem-minded group, though the article’s specific claims have not been independently checked here. Together the issue reads like a working club notebook for a platform finding its practical habits.

stories.headline: Home-Computer Forecasts Outrun the Console Market
body: Electronic Games cites an Electronics Industries Association estimate of 4.3 million home computers sold in 1983 at an average $440, and a forecast of 6.6 million in 1984 at an average $400. Those figures explain the pressure to put recognizable games on computer disks and cartridges.

The same report projects console unit sales down from 6.65 million in 1983 to 5 million in 1984. These are industry estimates and forecasts printed in October, not final audited results. For publishers preparing the next season, however, the direction of the forecast is enough to change the conversation.
